source.title: Multi-Objective Large Language Model Unlearning
source.authors: Zi-Bin Pan; Shu-Wen Zhang; Yuesheng Zheng; Chi-Ruei Li; Yu-Heng Cheng; Jun-Hua Zhao

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equations and symbols are imperfectly rendered, but the reported table values and relevant prose are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures unlearning outcomes and retained utility for several training-based methods, using harmful response rate and fluency rather than targeted-knowledge accuracy. It does not test whether attacks recover the behavior.
record.gate_note: No fine-tuning recovery attack, activation-direction ablation, quantization attack, or prompting-only recovery test is reported. Table I also reports toxicity and obscenity measures and update-direction conflict probabilities; these do not measure recovery by the attacks in versions B–E.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. It proposes MOLLM, an unlearning algorithm, and reports only its own method against baselines on harmful rate (HR) and fluency for Llama 3-8B on PKU-SafeRLHF. Its measure is harmful-response rate, not targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance. No recovery attack of any kind is run: no fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or prompting. So whether the suppression is shallow or deep cannot be judged, and no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the UCE loss avoids gradient explosion and that the common descent direction avoids catastrophic forgetting. They report MOLLM achieves the lowest HR, toxicity and obscenity with preserved fluency versus GA-based baselines. Results are the best over a learning-rate grid, on one model and one dataset, and no robustness to recovery attacks is examined.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes a training-based unlearning method using UCE loss and multi-objective common descent, and compares it with GA-based methods and other baselines. It does not reproduce or test post-unlearning recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different outcomes across unlearning methods and ablations; the smaller-learning-rate ablation has poorer results. It does not report attack-setting sensitivity.

fits_no_version.finding: On Llama 3-8B, unlearning methods cut PKU-SafeRLHF harmful rate from 79.18% to 3.4–5.7%. Retraining on the retain set only reaches 53.92%. GA-OGD and the CE-based ablations worsen fluency to 4.3–5.1, against 1.754 for the Original.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-ascent unlearning of harmful responses trades off against retained fluency unless gradient conflicts are resolved. This concerns suppression on the direct prompt, not deletion.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
record.problems: The reported target-behavior measure is harmful rate, not targeted-knowledge accuracy; no chance-level reference or uncertainty estimates are reported. The evaluation is on Llama 3-8B and the PKU-SafeRLHF dataset. No recovery attacks are tested.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's Table I also reports toxicity and obscenity for each method, and probabilities of update-direction conflict. These are omitted because the core claim versions concern targeted-knowledge recovery and retained general ability; the conflict probabilities do not measure either recovery or retained capability.

untested.parts: Targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance, and resistance to simple attacks; only HR and fluency are reported.
Recovery by relearning on unrelated, loosely related or forgotten data.
Recovery by activation-direction ablation, or analysis of blocking versus deletion.
Recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages or in-context information.
MOLLM is not claimed or tested to resist any recovery attack.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its version A labels are rejected. Every row is the study's own method or a baseline in its comparison. HR measures harmful outputs on direct prompts, which cannot separate shallow from deep unlearning without attacks. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper cites in-context unlearning being bypassed by prompt manipulation only as background (cites_only for E).

versions.untested_parts: The study measures harmful response rate and fluency after unlearning, but does not test targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance or whether simple attacks recover the behavior.
Recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
Recovery by ablating an activation direction, or evidence that a tested method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Whether a newer method resists recovery attacks.

reader_labels.reason: MOLLM lowers HR from 79.18% to 3.45% while fluency is 1.689 versus the Original 1.754; see r9–r10. This supports the measured unlearning-and-utility component only, not resistance to attacks.
